The flag of Tonga consists of a solid red field, a white square canton in the upper hoist, and a red Greek cross centered in that canton. When the image is discretized to an \(m \times n\) pixel grid, every red pixel receives the scalar value \(a\) and every white pixel receives the scalar value \(b\). The resulting matrix \(M\) therefore admits the decomposition
\[
M = (a-b)R + bJ,
\]
where \(R\) is the 0-1 indicator of the red pixels and \(J\) is the all-ones matrix (rank 1). Consequently
\[
\rank(M) \le \rank(R)+1.
\]
The geometry of the flag partitions the rows into at most four horizontal bands of constant pattern:
- the three bands created inside the canton by the horizontal arm of the cross,
- the single band lying entirely below the canton (solid red).

All rows belonging to the same band are identical, so \(M\) possesses at most four distinct row vectors. Hence its row space has dimension at most 4 and
\[
\rank(M)\le 4.
\]
For generic choices \(a\neq b\) and for sufficiently fine pixel grids that respect the band boundaries, the four distinct rows are linearly independent, showing that rank 4 is attained. Therefore the maximal possible rank is exactly 4.

\[
M = aJ + (b-a)W,
\]
where \(J\) is the all-ones matrix (rank 1) and \(W\) is the 0-1 indicator of the white region.

The white region itself is a rectangle minus a cross, hence the union of four smaller rectangles lying above, below, to the left, and to the right of the cross. The indicator of any single axis-aligned rectangle has rank 1, and the four rectangles share the same row-support and column-support; consequently \(\operatorname{rank}(W)\le 2\). \[
\operatorname{rank}(M)\le 1+2=3.
\]
The bound is tight: for any sufficiently fine discretization the three distinct row-types (entirely red rows below the canton, rows intersecting only the vertical arm of the cross, and rows intersecting the horizontal arm) are linearly independent, so \(\operatorname{rank}(M)=3\).

Hence the maximal possible rank is exactly 3.
